claim: C. tropicalis has seven pairs of chromosomes.
source: C. tropicalis has seven pairs of chromosomes (Chatterjee et al., 2016; Butler et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The current publicly available genome assembly (ASM633v3) has 23 nuclear contigs and one mitochondrial contig.
source: However, the current publicly available genome assembly (ASM633v3) has 23 nuclear contigs and one mitochondrial contig.
evidence: Refers to publicly available data

claim: Assembly2020 constitutes 14,609,527 bp in seven telomere-to-telomere long gapless chromosomes.
source: Finally, we used 3C-seq reads to polish the complete genome assembly of C. tropicalis constituting 14,609,527 bp in seven telomere-to-telomere long gapless chromosomes (Figure 1B).
evidence: Directly states the result of the assembly process

claim: In Assembly2020, 1278 out of 1315 Ascomycota-specific BUSCO gene sets could be identified compared to 1255 identified using Assembly A.
source: In Assembly2020, 1278 out of 1315 Ascomycota-specific BUSCO gene sets could be identified compared to 1255 identified using Assembly A (Supplementary file 4, Materials and methods).
evidence: Provides specific numerical data from BUSCO analysis

claim: The inclusion of 23 additional BUSCO gene sets suggests significantly improved contiguity and completeness of Assembly2020.
source: The inclusion of 23 additional BUSCO gene sets suggests significantly improved contiguity and completeness of Assembly2020.
evidence: Inference drawn from the BUSCO data comparison

claim: Chr4 homologs differed in size.
source: We observed that Chr4 homologs differed in size (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Observation from chromoblot analysis shown in figure

claim: An internal duplication of ~235 kb region on Chr4 could explain the size difference between the homologs Chr4A and Chr4B.
source: Analysis of the sequence coverage across Chr4 identified an internal duplication of ~235 kb region, which could explain the size difference between the homologs Chr4A and Chr4B (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Analysis of sequence coverage data

claim: Two additional large-scale duplication events were identified: one each on Chr5 (DUP5,~23 kb) and ChrR (DUPR,~80 kb).
source: Subsequently, we scanned the entire genome for the presence of copy number variations (CNVs), which led to the identification of two additional large-scale duplication events: one each on Chr5 (DUP5,~23 kb) and ChrR (DUPR,~80 kb) (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Results from genome-wide CNV scanning

claim: A balanced heterozygous translocation event between Chr1 and Chr4 was detected.
source: Additionally, we detected a balanced heterozygous translocation event between Chr1 and Chr4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A) through analyses of 3C-seq data and de novo contigs (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: Detected through 3C-seq data and de novo contig analysis

claim: The assembled length of ChrR is 2.1 Mb while the actual length from chromoblot analysis is ~2.8 Mb.
source: Thus, while chromoblot analysis suggests that the actual length of ChrR is ~2.8 Mb (Figure 1—figure supplement 5E), the assembled length is 2.1 Mb (Figure 1C).
evidence: Comparison of chromoblot and assembly data

claim: The difference between the assembled length and actual length of ChrR can be attributed to the presence of the repetitive rDNA locus of ~700 kb.
source: Considering the length of the rDNA locus is ~700 kb in C. albicans (Jones et al., 2004), we reason that the difference between the assembled length and actual length (derived from chromoblot analysis) of ChrR in C. tropicalis can be attributed to the presence of the repetitive rDNA locus of ~700 kb, which is not completely assembled in Assembly2020.
evidence: Inference based on known rDNA locus length in related species and assembly limitations

claim: A long chromosomal region depleted of SNPs and indels was detected on the left arm of ChrR.
source: Intriguingly, we detected a long chromosomal region depleted of SNPs and indels on the left arm of ChrR (Figure 1D).
evidence: Analysis of SNPs and indels from sequencing data

claim: Parts of the syntenic region of LOHR are SNP and indel depleted in C. sojae strain NCYC-2607 and C. albicans reference strain SC5314.
source: Strikingly, we found parts of the syntenic region of LOHR to be SNP and indel depleted in the C. sojae strain NCYC-2607, a closely related species of C. tropicalis, as well as in C. albicans reference strain SC5314 (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Comparative analysis across species

claim: Centromeres are clustered and localized at the periphery of the DAPI-stained nuclear DNA mass as a single punctum in C. tropicalis.
source: Indirect immunofluorescence imaging of the C. tropicalis strain (CtKS102) expressing Protein-A tagged CENP-ACse4 suggested that centromeres are clustered and localized at the periphery of the DAPI-stained nuclear DNA mass as a single punctum (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Direct observation from immunofluorescence microscopy

claim: Intrachromosomal interactions are generally stronger than interchromosomal interactions in C. tropicalis.
source: The resultant heatmap depicts high signal intensities along the diagonal, indicating that the intrachromosomal interactions are generally stronger than interchromosomal interactions, as observed before (Figure 2C; Duan et al., 2010).
evidence: Analysis of 3C-seq contact map data

claim: There is strong spatial proximity between centromeres in C. tropicalis.
source: However, the most striking feature of the heatmap is the presence of conspicuous puncta in the interchromosomal areas, which signify strong spatial proximity between centromeres (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: Interpretation of 3C-seq heatmap features

claim: Telomere-telomere interactions are enriched compared to neighboring regions in C. tropicalis.
source: Strikingly, we also noted the enrichment of telomere-telomere interactions as compared to the neighboring regions (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Analysis of 3C-seq data and aggregate signal analysis

claim: Interchromosomal telomeric interactions were significantly greater than all interchromosomal interactions (Mann-Whitney U test P value = 1.129⋅10−11).
source: Statistical comparison was then performed between these telomere-telomere interactions and bulk chromatin, which revealed that the interchromosomal telomeric interactions were significantly greater than the all interchromosomal interactions (Mann-Whitney U test P value = 1.129⋅10−11) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Statistical analysis of 3C-seq data

claim: Intrachromosomal telomeric interactions were significantly enhanced compared to all intrachromosomal long-range (>100 kb) interactions (Mann-Whitney U test P value = 7.374⋅10−11).
source: On the other hand, cis interactions between the two telomeres of an individual chromosome (intrachromosomal telomeric interactions) were also significantly enhanced compared to all intrachromosomal long-range (>100 kb) interactions (Mann-Whitney U test P value = 7.374⋅10−11) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Statistical analysis of 3C-seq data

claim: C. tropicalis chromosomes adopt the Rabl-like configuration.
source: All these lines of evidence prompted us to propose that C. tropicalis chromosomes adopt the Rabl-like configuration, a characteristic feature of the higher-order genome organization in yeasts (Duan et al., 2010; Descorps-Declère et al., 2015; Burrack et al., 2016).
evidence: Inference from multiple lines of 3C-seq evidence and comparison to known patterns

claim: Six out of seven centromeres (except CEN6) of C. tropicalis are located proximal to multiple ICSBs.
source: Considering the C. albicans genome as the reference, all four methods of analyses suggest that six out of seven centromeres (except CEN6) of C. tropicalis are located proximal to multiple ICSBs (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Results from four different synteny analysis methods

claim: A chromosomal region carrying three consecutive CtCEN6-proximal ORFs was lost in the C. albicans genome.
source: Although it appears that CtCEN6 escaped inter-centromeric translocations, synteny analysis suggested that a chromosomal region carrying three consecutive CtCEN6-proximal ORFs was lost in the C. albicans genome (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Synteny analysis comparing C. tropicalis and C. albicans

claim: Four out of seven centromeres (CEN2, CEN3, CEN5, and CENR) in C. tropicalis are precisely located at the ICSBs.
source: ORF-level synteny analysis further revealed that four out of seven centromeres (CEN2, CEN3, CEN5, and CENR) in C. tropicalis are precisely located at the ICSBs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), while multiple ICSBs are located within ~100 kb of other two centromeres (Figure 3A).
evidence: ORF-level synteny analysis

claim: A convergence of orthoblocks from as many as four different chromosomes of C. albicans was detected within 100 kb of C. tropicalis centromeres.
source: Additionally, a convergence of orthoblocks from as many as four different chromosomes of C. albicans was detected within 100 kb of C. tropicalis centromeres (Figure 3B).
evidence: Analysis of orthoblock distribution

claim: All centromeres of C. albicans, except CaCEN2, were found to be associated with ICSBs when using the C. tropicalis genome as the reference.
source: It is important to note that by using the C. tropicalis genome as the reference, all centromeres of C. albicans, except CaCEN2, were found to be associated with ICSBs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Reciprocal synteny analysis

claim: The ICSB density is maximum at the centromere-proximal zones for all six chromosomes, but drops sharply at the chromosomal arms.
source: Our analysis reveals that the ICSB density is maximum at the centromere-proximal zones for all six chromosomes, but drops sharply at the chromosomal arms.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of ICSB distribution across chromosomes

claim: The ICSB density near the telomere-proximal zone for Chr2, Chr4, and ChrR shows an increase compared to the chromosomal arms.
source: However, the ICSB density near the telomere-proximal zone for Chr2, Chr4, and ChrR shows an increase compared to the chromosomal arms, albeit at a lower magnitude than centromeres.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of ICSB distribution

claim: The lengths of the orthoblocks located proximal to centromeres and telomeres are significantly smaller than orthoblocks located at the centromere-/telomere-distal zones.
source: This analysis further reveals that the lengths of the orthoblocks located proximal to centromeres and telomeres are significantly smaller than orthoblocks located at the centromere-/telomere-distal zones (Figure 3D).
evidence: Statistical comparison of orthoblock lengths across genomic zones

claim: At least ten loci were identified where a convergence of C. tropicalis ORFs from different chromosomes had taken place in C. albicans.
source: Indeed, we identified at least ten loci where a convergence of C. tropicalis ORFs from different chromosomes had taken place in C. albicans (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Synteny analysis of ORF convergence

claim: Four loci showing convergence of C. tropicalis ORFs are proximal to the centromeres (CEN3, CEN4, CEN7, and CENR) in C. albicans.
source: Intriguingly, we found four such loci that are proximal to the centromeres (CEN3, CEN4, CEN7, and CENR) in C. albicans (Figure 3E–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: Detailed synteny analysis near centromeres

claim: Inter-centromeric translocation events may have occurred in the common ancestor of C. albicans and C. tropicalis.
source: This observation strongly supports the possibility of inter-centromeric translocation events in the common ancestor of C. albicans and C. tropicalis.
evidence: Inference from synteny analysis showing ORF convergence patterns

claim: The other four centromeres in C. albicans are located proximal to ORFs, orthologs of which are also proximal to the centromeres in C. tropicalis.
source: Additionally, the other four centromeres in C. albicans are located proximal to ORFs, orthologs of which are also proximal to the centromeres in C. tropicalis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Synteny analysis of centromere-proximal regions

claim: The ancestral HIR-associated centromeres were lost in C. albicans, and ENCs formed proximal to the ancestral centromere loci on unique DNA sequences.
source: We posit that the ancestral HIR-associated centromeres were lost in C. albicans, and ENCs formed proximal to the ancestral centromere loci on unique DNA sequences.
evidence: Hypothesis based on synteny patterns and centromere type differences

claim: Eight HIR-associated structures were identified in the reference genome of C. parapsilosis strain CDC317 (ASM18276v2).
source: Indeed, we identified eight HIR-associated structures, in the reference genome of C. parapsilosis strain CDC317 (ASM18276v2).
evidence: Analysis of C. parapsilosis genome assembly

claim: The HIR-associated structures in C. parapsilosis are located at intergenic and transcription-poor regions, one each on all eight chromosomes.
source: Identification of the HIR-associated structures present at the intergenic and transcription-poor regions, one each on all eight chromosomes, suggests that these loci are the putative centromeres of C. parapsilosis.
evidence: Characterization of HIR-associated structures in genome

claim: All eight CENP-ACse4 enriched centromeres in the CLIB214 strain of C. parapsilosis are located at HIR-associated loci.
source: Indeed, it was recently reported that all eight CENP-ACse4 enriched centromeres in the CLIB214 strain of C. parapsilosis are located at HIR-associated loci (Ola et al., 2020).
evidence: Citation to recent publication

claim: The common ancestor of C. albicans and C. tropicalis possibly carried HIR-associated centromeres.
source: Based on these lines of evidence, we conclude that the common ancestor of C. albicans and C. tropicalis possibly carried HIR-associated centromeres.
evidence: Inference from comparative analysis across species

claim: Two centromeres in another isolate (90-137) of C. parapsilosis have been shown to be formed on non-HIR-associated loci.
source: Surprisingly, two centromeres in another isolate (90-137) of C. parapsilosis have been shown to be formed on non-HIR-associated loci (Ola et al., 2020).
evidence: Citation to published study

claim: IRs are present in CEN4, CEN5, and CENR of C. albicans, but these sequences are not homogenized like the HIR-associated centromeres in C. tropicalis.
source: Although IRs are present in CEN4, CEN5, and CENR of C. albicans, these sequences are not homogenized like the HIR-associated centromeres in C. tropicalis (Figure 4A).
evidence: Comparative sequence analysis

claim: The genome of C. sojae (NCYC-2607) was assembled into 42 contigs, including seven chromosome-length contigs.
source: To study the presence of HIRs in C. sojae (NCYC-2607), a sister species of C. tropicalis (Shen et al., 2018), we assembled its genome into 42 contigs, including seven chromosome-length contigs (Materials and methods).
evidence: Results of genome assembly

claim: Seven putative centromeres were identified in C. sojae as intergenic and HIR-associated loci syntenic to the centromeres in C. tropicalis.
source: Using this assembly, we identified seven putative centromeres in C. sojae as intergenic and HIR-associated loci syntenic to the centromeres in C. tropicalis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Synteny analysis and structural characterization

claim: Each of the seven putative centromeres in C. sojae consists of a ~2 kb long CC region flanked by 3–12 kb long inverted repeats.
source: Each of these seven putative centromeres in C. sojae consists of a ~2 kb long CC region flanked by 3–12 kb long inverted repeats (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Structural analysis of putative centromeres

claim: Six HIR-associated centromeres were identified in the publicly available genome assembly (ASM332773v1) of C. viswanathii.
source: Using a similar approach, we identified six HIR-associated centromeres in the publicly available genome assembly (ASM332773v1) of Candida viswanathii, another species closely related to C. tropicalis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–E, Supplementary file 6; Tsui et al., 2008).
evidence: Analysis of public genome assembly

claim: Homologous sequences are shared across IRs but not among the CC elements of the HIR-associated centromeres in C. tropicalis, C. sojae, and C. viswanathii.
source: A dot-plot analysis identified the presence of homologous sequences shared across IRs but not among the CC elements (Figure 4A) of the HIR-associated centromeres present in C. tropicalis and the putative centromeres of C. sojae and C. viswanathii (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: Dot-plot sequence comparison analysis

claim: Extensive structural conservation in centromere DNA elements, especially among IRs, exists within an individual species.
source: Moreover, we detected extensive structural conservation in centromere DNA elements, especially among IRs within an individual species (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Structural analysis of centromere elements

claim: Structural features of IRs are significantly conserved across the three species, C. tropicalis, C. sojae, and C. viswanathii.
source: These structural feature of IRs are also significantly conserved across the three species, C. tropicalis, C. sojae, and C. viswanathii (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Comparative structural analysis across species

claim: A highly conserved 12-bp motif (IR-motif) was identified in centromere DNA sequences.
source: This analysis identified a highly conserved 12-bp motif (dubbed as IR-motif) (Figure 4B) clustered specifically at centromeres but not anywhere else in the entire genome of C. tropicalis, C. sojae and C. viswanathii (Figure 4C–D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Motif discovery analysis of centromere sequences

claim: The IR-motif density at centromeres in C. albicans remains approximately an order of magnitude lower than that of C. tropicalis.
source: On the contrary, the IR-motif density at centromeres in C. albicans remains approximately an order of magnitude lower than that of C. tropicalis (Figure 4C).
evidence: Comparative analysis of motif density

claim: The IR-motif indicates a potential function in the regulation of de novo CENP-ACse4 loading in C. tropicalis.
source: This observation indicates a potential function of IR-motifs in the regulation of de novo CENP-ACse4 loading in C. tropicalis.
evidence: Inference from motif enrichment pattern

claim: The CEN-enriched motif found at IRs is absent at central core region in C. tropicalis.
source: Moreover, this CEN-enriched motif found at IRs is absent at central core region in C. tropicalis (Figure 4E) and at the putative centromeres in C. sojae and C. viswanathii (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Analysis of motif distribution within centromeres

claim: The direction of the IR-motif is diverging away from the central core in C. tropicalis, C. sojae, and C. viswanathii.
source: Additionally, we noted that the direction of the IR-motif is diverging away from the central core in C. tropicalis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E) as well as in the other two species (Figure 4—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Analysis of motif orientation

claim: The conserved structure and organization of the IR-motif sequences in the HIR-associated centromeres of three Candida species suggest an inter-species conserved function of the IR DNA sequence.
source: The conserved structure and organization of the IR-motif sequences in the HIR-associated centromeres of three Candida species suggest an inter-species conserved function of the IR DNA sequence.
evidence: Inference from comparative analysis of motif conservation

claim: The clusters of IR-motifs are located at a variable distance from CC in C. tropicalis, C. sojae, and C. viswanathii.
source: However, the clusters of IR-motifs are located at a variable distance from CC in these species (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: Analysis of motif positioning relative to central core

claim: Three large-scale duplication events and few small-scale CNV loci were identified in the C. tropicalis genome.
source: We further identified three large-scale duplication events and few small-scale CNV loci in its genome, phased the diploid genome of C. tropicalis, and mapped SNPs and indels.
evidence: Results from genome analysis

claim: Significant centromere-centromere as well as telomere-telomere spatial interactions were identified in C. tropicalis.
source: We constructed a genome-wide chromatin contact map and identified significant centromere-centromere as well as telomere-telomere spatial interactions.
evidence: Analysis of 3C-seq data

claim: ORFs proximal to the centromeres of C. tropicalis are converged into specific regions on the C. albicans genome.
source: Strikingly, ORFs proximal to the centromeres of C. tropicalis are converged into specific regions on the C. albicans genome, suggesting that inter-centromeric translocations may have occurred in their common ancestor.
evidence: Synteny analysis results

claim: The presence of HIR-associated putative centromeres in C. sojae and C. viswanathii suggests that such a centromere structure is plausibly the ancestral form in the CUG-Ser1 clade.
source: Moreover, the presence of HIR-associated putative centromeres in C. sojae and C. viswanathii, like in C. tropicalis, suggests that such a centromere structure is plausibly the ancestral form in the CUG-Ser1 clade but lost both in C. albicans and C. dubliniensis.
evidence: Inference from comparative analysis across species

claim: Loss of HIR-associated centromere structure might have occurred during translocation events involving centromeres of homologous DNA sequences in the common ancestor.
source: We propose that loss of such a centromere structure might have occurred during translocation events involving centromeres of homologous DNA sequences in the common ancestor, to give rise to ENCs on unique DNA sequences and facilitated speciation.
evidence: Proposed model based on multiple lines of evidence

claim: A double-stranded DNA break at CEN6 followed by the fusion of broken ends could explain the loss of three ORFs.
source: This observation can be explained by a double-stranded DNA break at the centromere followed by the fusion of broken ends resulting in the loss of those ORFs.
evidence: Proposed mechanism to explain observed pattern

claim: C. tropicalis is a human pathogenic ascomycete, closely related to C. albicans.
source: C. tropicalis is a human pathogenic ascomycete, closely related to the well-studied model fungal pathogen C. albicans (Legrand et al., 2019).
evidence: Established taxonomic relationship

claim: C. tropicalis and C. albicans diverged from their common ancestor ~39 million years ago.
source: These two species diverged from their common ancestor ~39 million years ago (Kumar et al., 2017) and evolved with distinct karyotypes (Chatterjee et al., 2016), having different phenotypic traits (Cavalheiro and Teixeira, 2018), and ecological niches (Pappas et al., 2018).
evidence: Citation to phylogenetic study

claim: Systemic ICU-acquired candidiasis is primarily (30.5–41.6%) caused by C. tropicalis in tropical countries including India, Pakistan, and Brazil.
source: While C. albicans remains the primary cause of candidiasis worldwide, systemic ICU-acquired candidiasis is primarily (30.5–41.6%) caused by C. tropicalis in tropical countries including India (Chakrabarti et al., 2015), Pakistan (Farooqi et al., 2013), and Brazil (da Costa et al., 2014).
evidence: Citations to epidemiological studies

claim: The occurrence of drug resistance, particularly multidrug resistance, in C. tropicalis is on the rise.
source: Moreover, the occurrence of drug resistance, particularly multidrug resistance, in C. tropicalis is on the rise (Chakrabarti et al., 2015; Xiao et al., 2015; Gonçalves et al., 2016).
evidence: Citations to studies on drug resistance

claim: C. tropicalis is emerging as a major threat for nosocomial candidemia with 29–72% broad spectrum mortality rate.
source: Therefore, relatively less-studied C. tropicalis is emerging as a major threat for nosocomial candidemia with 29–72% broad spectrum mortality rate (Lamoth et al., 2018).
evidence: Citation to clinical study

claim: Fluconazole resistance in C. albicans can be gained due to segmental aneuploidy of Chr5 containing long IRs at the centromere, by the formation of isochromosomes.
source: Fluconazole resistance in C. albicans can be gained due to segmental aneuploidy of Chr5 containing long IRs at the centromere, by the formation of isochromosomes (Selmecki et al., 2006), which was also identified in Chr4 with IRs at its centromere (Todd et al., 2019).
evidence: Citations to studies on drug resistance mechanisms

claim: All seven centromeres in C. tropicalis are associated with long IRs with the potential to form isochromosomes.
source: All seven centromeres in C. tropicalis are associated with long IRs with the potential to form isochromosomes.
evidence: Inference from structural characterization of centromeres

claim: The mechanism of homology search during HR is positively influenced by spatial proximity and the extent of DNA sequence homology.
source: Since the mechanism of homology search during HR is positively influenced by spatial proximity and the extent of DNA sequence homology (Agmon et al., 2013; Seeber et al., 2018), at least in the engineered model systems, it is expected that spatially clustered homologous DNA sequences undergo more translocation events than other loci.
evidence: Citations to studies on homologous recombination

claim: The bipolar to the tetrapolar transition of the mating type locus in the Cryptococcus species complex was associated with inter-centromeric recombination following pericentric inversion.
source: For example, the bipolar to the tetrapolar transition of the mating type locus in the Cryptococcus species complex was associated with inter-centromeric recombination following pericentric inversion (Sun et al., 2017).
evidence: Citation to study on Cryptococcus

claim: Inter-centromeric recombination has been reported in the common ancestor of two fission yeast species, S. cryophilus and S. octosporus.
source: Similar inter-centromeric recombination has been reported in the common ancestor of two fission yeast species, Schizosaccharomyces cryophilus and Schizosaccharomyces octosporus (Tong et al., 2019).
evidence: Citation to study on fission yeast

claim: Centromeres serve as sites of recombination, which may lead to centromere loss and/or the emergence of ENCs.
source: These examples raise an intriguing notion that centromeres serve as sites of recombination, which may lead to centromere loss and/or the emergence of ENCs.
evidence: Inference from multiple examples across species

claim: DSBs at centromeres following fusion of the acentric fragments to other chromosomes led to chromosome number reduction in Ashbya species and Malassezia species.
source: This notion is supported by the fact that DSBs at centromeres following fusion of the acentric fragments to other chromosomes led to chromosome number reduction in Ashbya species (Gordon et al., 2011) and Malassezia species (Sankaranarayanan et al., 2020).
evidence: Citations to studies on chromosome evolution

claim: Genomic instability at the centromere can lead to fluconazole resistance, as in the case of isochromosome formation on Chr5 of C. albicans.
source: Genomic instability at the centromere can also lead to fluconazole resistance, as in the case of isochromosome formation on Chr5 of C. albicans (Selmecki et al., 2006).
evidence: Citation to study on drug resistance

claim: Breaks at the centromeres were reported to be associated with cancers in humans.
source: Additionally, breaks at the centromeres were reported to be associated with cancers in humans (Barra and Fachinetti, 2018).
evidence: Citation to study on cancer

claim: Interchromosomal contacts between chromosome pairs have been correlated with the number of translocation events in both naturally occurring populations and experimentally induced mammalian cells.
source: interchromosomal contacts between chromosome pairs have been correlated with the number of translocation events in both naturally occurring populations and experimentally induced mammalian cells (Arsuaga et al., 2004; Bickmore and Teague, 2002; Branco and Pombo, 2006; Canela et al., 2017; Engreitz et al., 2012; Hlatky et al., 2002; Holley et al., 2002; Klein et al., 2011; Roukos et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Multiple citations to studies on chromosome contacts and translocations

claim: Contacts between various chromosomal territories as well as their relative positions in the nucleus influence the sites and frequency of translocation events both in flies and mammals.
source: It has been suggested that contacts between various chromosomal territories as well as their relative positions in the nucleus influence the sites and frequency of translocation events both in flies and mammals (Engreitz et al., 2012; Aten et al., 2004; Foster et al., 2013; Savage, 1998; Savage, 2000; Meaburn, 2016).
evidence: Citations to studies on nuclear organization and translocations

claim: Robertsonian translocation (RT) involving fusion between arms of two different chromosomes near a centromere is the most frequently detected chromosomal abnormality in humans.
source: Nevertheless, one of the well-studied translocation events, Robertsonian translocation (RT) involving fusion between arms of two different chromosomes near a centromere, is the most frequently detected chromosomal abnormality in humans (Therman et al., 1989).
evidence: Citation to study on human chromosomal abnormalities

claim: The occurrence of RT was first reported in grasshoppers and subsequently it has been implicated in the karyotype evolution in humans, mice, and wheat.
source: The occurrence of RT was first reported in grasshoppers (Robertson, 1916) and subsequently it has been implicated in the karyotype evolution in humans (Therman et al., 1989), mice (Castiglia and Capanna, 2002; Dumas and Britton-Davidian, 2002), and wheat (Friebe et al., 2005).
evidence: Citations to studies on Robertsonian translocations across species

claim: RTs cause sterility in humans, are often linked with the heterogeneity of carcinomas, and are implicated in genetic disorders.
source: Moreover, RTs cause sterility in humans (Guichaoua et al., 1990), often linked with the heterogeneity of carcinomas (Hermsen et al., 2005), and implicated in genetic disorders (Mattei et al., 1984).
evidence: Citations to clinical studies

claim: Cytological and Hi-C based evidence of spatial proximity among the repeat-associated centromere DNA sequences in humans, mice, and wheat supports a possibility that RTs may have been guided by spatial proximity.
source: Intriguingly, cytological and Hi-C based evidence (Imakaev et al., 2012) of spatial proximity (reviewed in Muller et al., 2019) among the repeat-associated centromere DNA sequences (Kalitsis et al., 2006) in these species supports a possibility that RTs may have been guided by spatial proximity.
evidence: Citations to studies on spatial organization and inference about RT mechanism

claim: Chromoplexy, involving a series of translocation events among multiple chromosomes without alterations in the copy number, was identified in prostate cancers.
source: Similarly, chromoplexy, involving a series of translocation events among multiple chromosomes without alterations in the copy number, was identified in prostate cancers (Zhang et al., 2013; Baca et al., 2013).
evidence: Citations to cancer genomics studies

claim: The growing evidence that chromoplexy events are associated with the formation of micronuclei supports the idea that the spatial genome organization may influence chromoplexy.
source: Although fine mapping of translocation events at the repetitive regions in human cancer cells is challenging, the growing evidence that such events are associated with the formation of micronuclei (Crasta et al., 2012) supports the idea that the spatial genome organization may influence chromoplexy as well (Meaburn et al., 2007).
evidence: Citations to studies and inference about mechanism

claim: The unique centromeres might have evolved from an ancestral HIR-associated centromere.
source: The identification of HIR-associated putative centromeres in C. parapsilosis, C. sojae, and C. viswanathii supports the idea that the unique centromeres might have evolved from an ancestral HIR-associated centromere (Coughlan et al., 2016; Figure 5A).
evidence: Inference from comparative analysis across species

claim: HIR-associated centromeres of C. tropicalis, C. sojae, and C. viswanathii form on different DNA sequences.
source: While HIR-associated centromeres of C. tropicalis, C. sojae, and C. viswanathii form on different DNA sequences, a well-conserved IR-motif was identified in this study that is present in multiple copies on the centromeric IR sequences across these three species.
evidence: Comparative sequence analysis

claim: Some centromeres in C. albicans carry chromosome-specific IRs but lack IR-motifs.
source: Some centromeres in C. albicans carry chromosome-specific IRs but lack IR-motifs.
evidence: Analysis of C. albicans centromere sequences

claim: CaCEN5 IRs could not functionally complement the centromere function in C. tropicalis for the de novo CENP-ACse4 recruitment.
